passage:
Subject: Revised timelines for the brand rollout

Dear Ritu,

Thank you for trusting us with the whole rollout. Last week I said yes to the packaging, the website, the launch video and the social calendar, all by the 20th. I've looked at my schedule honestly, and I can't deliver all four at the quality you deserve.

Here's what I can promise: packaging and website by the 20th, the video by the 5th of next month, and the social calendar in the same week. If the video needs to come sooner, I'd suggest a shorter version now and a longer one later.

I should have said this at the start. I was afraid of losing the project, and I overpromised. From now on I'll give you dates I can keep.

Warm regards,
Kalyani

qa.q: Which four items did Kalyani agree to deliver by the 20th?
qa.a: Kalyani had agreed to the packaging, the website, the launch video and the social calendar.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani say yes to everything at first?
qa.a: Kalyani was afraid of losing a big client and overpromised, as the email admits.

qa.q: What could Kalyani do to avoid overpromising in future?
qa.a: Kalyani could give timelines that can actually be kept, say what is possible up front and, over time, build a wider set of clients so no single one holds so much fear.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel on reading the revised timeline?
qa.a: Ritu may be a little disappointed about the delay but probably appreciates the honesty and the useful option of a shorter video first.

grounding: Fearing loss of a big client, Kalyani said yes to everything; the email corrects the overpromise with honest, keepable timelines.

passage:
Coaching note, session 4.
Pooja arrived late, eyes red. She runs a four-person design studio in Pune, and Zubin's retail chain is half her income. Last week Zubin asked for fifty store banners in three days. She said yes. She also said yes to a new website "by month end" and weekend calls.
She has slept five hours a night for two weeks. Two banners went out with the wrong prices, and Zubin was angry anyway.
She said, "If I say no, he'll leave. Then what?"
I asked what she could actually deliver well. She worked it out: twenty banners in three days, the rest by next Wednesday; the website in six weeks, not four. We practised how to say it: "Here's what I can do well, and when."
We also talked about finding two smaller clients over the next few months, so one client doesn't hold her whole studio.
She called Zubin from my office. He agreed to the new dates.

qa.q: How much of Pooja's income comes from Zubin's retail chain?
Why did Pooja keep saying yes to Zubin?
qa.a: She was afraid of losing him, and worried that without Zubin the studio would not survive.

qa.q: What did the coach help Pooja do?
qa.a: Work out what she could deliver well, practise offering realistic timelines, and plan to find two smaller clients over time.

qa.q: How might Zubin see the new dates?
qa.a: Zubin may be surprised but relieved to get reliable work after the wrong-price banners, which is why he agrees.

grounding: Afraid of losing a big client, the protagonist says yes to everything until quality and health suffer; she learns to offer realistic timelines and plans to diversify.

passage:
Chandrika's diary, Thursday, 1 a.m.
Disha asked for the whole brochure in Tamil AND Hindi by Monday. I said "Of course, no problem!" in that bright voice I use when I'm panicking.
She's my biggest client. If she walks, rent is gone.
But I've already promised three other things this week. I haven't eaten dinner. My neck hurts from sitting. Last month I sent her a translation with two mistakes because I was this tired, and she noticed.
I'm scared of her. That's the truth. Not of her exactly, of losing her.
So tomorrow, first thing, I'm calling her. Script:
"I can do Tamil by Monday, done properly. Hindi by Thursday. If you need both Monday, I'd rather tell you now than do it badly."
Also: I'm messaging that school that asked for translations last month. One client shouldn't feel like my whole life.
Going to sleep. Actually going.

qa.q: What languages did Disha ask for the brochure in?
What was Chandrika feeling when saying "Of course, no problem!"?
qa.a: Chandrika was panicking and scared of losing the biggest client, hiding it behind a bright voice.

qa.q: What is Chandrika's plan to stop overpromising?
qa.a: Calling Disha with a realistic timeline, Tamil by Monday and Hindi by Thursday, and contacting another potential client to spread the risk.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt about last month's translation mistakes?
qa.a: Disha probably felt annoyed and less confident in the work, which is why an honest timeline may rebuild trust.

grounding: Afraid of losing a big client, the protagonist says yes to everything and the work suffers; she plans to give honest timelines and diversify clients.
